terms.grammar: phrase: aliquem in hostium numerō habēre, to count someone among the enemy
evidence: Caes. BG 1.28.1: aliquem in hostium numerō (Lewis & Short s.v. habeō)
Cic. N. D. 1.36: aliquem in deōrum numerō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To lump one person in with others is, in Latin, to count him in their number: the group goes into the genitive after numerō. The passive is common: hostium numerō habērī, to be counted as an enemy (Cic. Att. 11.6.6, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: coin more, add to a sum (not “lump together”)
evidence: Traupman 103: lump s.o. together with, aliquem accūdō (+ dat.)
Plaut. Merc. 2.3.96: trīs minās accūdere etiam possum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives the verb only as “to coin further, to add to a sum of money”, from its one passage in Plautus; nothing supports the sense “lump together” with a dative.

sources: Lewis & Short: habeo · Lewis & Short: accudo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 103.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
